integrations/backend-orchestration:
Your backend is the control plane for products built on MIOSA. It owns the user
session, product permissions, billing policy, model routing, agent roster,
connector grants, and approval rules. MIOSA owns the execution substrate:
sandboxes, computers, files, exec, previews, artifacts, events, snapshots, and
deployments.

Use this guide when you are building products like app builders, artifact
workspaces, Polsia-style operators, Cofounder / Co-Founder AI-style company
agents, Nebula-style virtual devices, or Heuresis-style encoded workspaces.

> **Note: Keep keys server-side**
>
> Use tenant or workspace API keys from your backend. Browsers should receive
> short-lived browser tokens, preview tokens, or your own session-bound proxy
> responses. Do not put `msk_*` keys in client code.

---

## Backend responsibilities

- **Resolve ownership**: Map your account, workspace, user, project, document, or app record to MIOSA
  ownership fields before creating resources.
- **Choose the runtime**: Route work to a sandbox for code/files, a computer for browser/desktop, or a
  local device when customer-owned hardware is required.
- **Dispatch the prompt**: Send the user's task into the selected agent runtime and assigned device.
  The agent should work inside that device, not build locally and upload later.
- **Stream progress**: Normalize tool calls, command output, file writes, screenshots, preview
  readiness, artifacts, approvals, and final URLs into one product event stream.
- **Persist outputs**: Store MIOSA resource ids, artifact ids, snapshot ids, deployment ids,
  connector grant ids, and request ids next to your own product records.
- **Enforce policy**: Apply quota, budget, approval, network, and connector rules before the agent
  can spend credits, send messages, publish apps, or use sensitive credentials.

---

## Reference flow

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant User
  participant App as Your backend
  participant Queue
  participant Agent
  participant S as MIOSA sandbox
  participant C as MIOSA computer
  participant UI as Your frontend

  User->>App: prompt
  App->>App: authorize, resolve workspace/project/user
  App->>S: create or resume runtime
  App->>Queue: enqueue agent run
  Queue->>Agent: assigned runtime + device + scoped tools
  Agent->>S: write files and run commands in /workspace
  S-->>App: events, stdout, file changes, preview URL
  Agent->>C: browser QA when needed
  C-->>App: screenshots and browser events
  App-->>UI: normalized live run stream
  Agent->>S: publish or create artifacts
  App-->>User: artifact, preview, or deployment URL
```

The important boundary is simple: your backend orchestrates; the agent executes
inside a MIOSA device.

---

## Prompt dispatch contract

Model every agent run as a prompt dispatched into an assigned device.

```typescript
type DevicePromptDispatch = {
  tenantId: string;
  workspaceId: string;
  projectId?: string;
  userId: string;
  deviceType: "sandbox" | "computer" | "local";
  deviceId: string;
  runtime: "osa" | "codex" | "claude-code" | "hermes" | "gemini-cli" | "opencode" | "custom";
  prompt: string;
  cwd?: string;
  connectors?: string[];
  approvalPolicy: "auto" | "confirm-risky" | "manual";
  idempotencyKey: string;
};
```

The output stream should use one shape even when runtimes differ:

| Event | Use it for |
|---|---|
| `run.started` | The backend accepted the prompt and assigned a device |
| `tool.started` / `tool.completed` | Agent tool calls, MCP calls, connector calls |
| `command.output` | stdout/stderr from sandbox or computer commands |
| `file.changed` | Files created, edited, renamed, or deleted |
| `preview.ready` | Live server URL is ready |
| `artifact.created` | PDF, DOCX, image, HTML, ZIP, report, screenshot, or generated code output |
| `approval.required` | The agent wants to do something sensitive |
| `deployment.ready` | Stable public app URL is available |
| `run.failed` | Typed failure with request id and recovery path |

---

## Backend resource model

Store both your product ids and MIOSA ids. Do not force users or agents to
discover partial state after a retry.

```sql
agent_runs
  id
  tenant_id
  workspace_id
  project_id
  user_id
  prompt
  runtime
  device_type
  device_id
  sandbox_id
  computer_id
  deployment_id
  status
  idempotency_key
  created_at
  updated_at

agent_run_events
  id
  run_id
  type
  payload_json
  request_id
  created_at

agent_artifacts
  id
  run_id
  miosa_artifact_id
  path
  content_type
  size_bytes
  preview_url
  download_url
  created_at
```

For generated app products, also store the current persistent sandbox and latest
deployment per project:

```sql
projects
  id
  current_sandbox_id
  current_computer_id
  current_deployment_id
  primary_device_type
  primary_device_id
```

---

## SDK shape

Use the SDK language that matches your backend. The product logic is the same in
every language.

- [TypeScript backend](/docs/sdks/typescript): Node, Next.js route handlers, queues, AI SDK harnesses, and product backends.
- [Python backend](/docs/sdks/python): FastAPI, Django, Flask, data jobs, artifact generation, and Python agent loops.
- [Go backend](/docs/sdks/go): High-concurrency orchestration services, workers, queues, and control planes.
- [Elixir backend](/docs/sdks/elixir): Phoenix control planes, LiveView progress streams, queues, and long-running orchestration.

The minimum backend loop:

```text
1. Authenticate your user.
2. Resolve their workspace/project/user attribution.
3. Create or resume a sandbox/computer.
4. Dispatch the prompt into that device.
5. Stream events back to your UI.
6. Store artifacts, snapshots, previews, and deployments.
7. Enforce budget, quota, connector, and approval policy.
```

---

## Recovery rules

Production backends need to recover from partial progress.

| Failure | Backend behavior |
|---|---|
| Create succeeded, upload failed | Return the sandbox id and retry command; do not hide the partial resource |
| Agent runtime crashed | Keep the device and events; let user retry into the same workspace |
| Preview failed | Surface logs and process state; do not delete files automatically |
| Sandbox stopped | Resume or fork from snapshot when persistence is available |
| Budget exceeded | Stop new work and show the usage source |
| Connector authorization missing | Return a connect-account action, not a generic 500 |
| Publish failed | Keep the sandbox preview and release artifact for retry |

Use idempotency keys on mutations so retries do not create duplicate sandboxes,
deployments, or app records.

---

## See also

- [Build an agent-company platform](/docs/guides/build-agent-company): Product architecture for Polsia, Cofounder, Nebula, and Heuresis-style systems.
- [Agent orchestration](/docs/guides/agent-orchestration): Scale from one agent to thousands with queues, devices, subagents, and events.
- [API reference](/docs/api-reference): Low-level REST endpoints for sandboxes, computers, files, exec, events, and deploys.
- [White-label SaaS walkthrough](/docs/platform/white-label): Customer attribution, preview tokens, custom domains, and branded product flows.
integrations/comparison:
This page compares **compute price** across the platforms customers evaluate against MIOSA.
Every MIOSA figure is from its live pricing API and its published price per size.
Every competitor figure is from the vendor's own pricing page, checked **2026-10-20**, with the source listed at the end.

For capabilities and measured performance, see [MIOSA vs other platforms](/docs/compare).
That section is the current, verified comparison, and this page does not repeat it.

**MIOSA**
  Freestyle
  E2B
  Railway
  Vercel Sandbox

## Pricing model

| Provider | Model | Entry price | Free tier |
|---|---|---|---|
| **MIOSA** | One published price per size, metered by the second; plans set what is included and a size ceiling | Free $0 · Developer $20/mo · Business $500/mo · Enterprise $2,000/mo | Free: $1 of usage every month, no card needed |
| **Freestyle** | Subscription plus hourly usage | Hobby $50/mo | Free plan; the included allowance resets every month |
| **E2B** | Subscription plus per-second usage | Pro $150/mo | Hobby: free, plus a one-time $100 credit |
| **Railway** | Subscription credited against usage | Pro $20/mo, credited | not compared here |
| **Vercel Sandbox** | Usage on top of a Pro seat | Pro $20/mo credit plus a $20 seat | not compared here |

## Compute cost, normalized

Same box everywhere: **4 vCPU / 8 GiB RAM, running, per hour**, computed from each vendor's published unit rates.
MIOSA figures come from the live pricing API (`GET /api/v1/pricing`): each size has one hourly price, and the 4 vCPU / 8 GiB size is $0.1785.

| Provider | vCPU rate | RAM rate | **4 vCPU + 8 GiB / hr** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **MIOSA** | $0.027216 / vCPU-hr | $0.0087075 / GiB-hr | **$0.1785** (compute only; disk and egress metered separately) |
| **Railway** | $0.02779 / vCPU-hr | $0.01389 / GiB-hr | **~$0.22** |
| **Freestyle** | $0.04032 / vCPU-hr | $0.0129 / GiB-hr | **~$0.26** |
| **E2B** | $0.0504 / vCPU-hr | $0.0162 / GiB-hr | **~$0.33** (+ $150/mo on Pro) |
| **Vercel Sandbox** | $0.128 / active vCPU-hr | $0.0212 / GB-hr | **~$0.68** (active CPU only) |

> **Note**
>
> These are list prices for running compute only, and they move.
> MIOSA also meters disk and network egress; several providers bill storage, egress, and higher multi-region rates on top.
> Vercel bills CPU only while it is active.
> Size the shape you care about in the calculator below.

## Cost calculator

Drag to size a box and see the estimated monthly cost per provider, computed live from the list rates above.

vCPU **4** RAM **8 GiB** Hours per month **160 h**

| Provider | Est. monthly | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| MIOSAus | $29 | One published price per size on every plan; Developer has no monthly minimum |
| Railway | $36 | Containers; volumes $0.15/GB-month; egress $0.05/GB; Pro $20/mo credited |
| Freestyle | $42 | Free tier; Hobby $50/mo; storage $0.0628/GiB-month; egress $0.02/GB |
| E2B | $53 | Hobby free plus a $100 credit; Pro $150/mo; a desktop is a standard sandbox |
| Vercel | $109 | Bills active CPU only; egress $0.15/GB; Pro $20/mo credit plus a $20 seat |

Everything scales with the box you size above, at each provider's published list rates. MIOSA bills one published price per size on every plan, so the figure is the size price while the machine runs and not a plan price; disk and egress are metered separately. Competitor numbers are each vendor's public pricing as of 2026-10-11. Verify them before you rely on them.

## Where MIOSA fits best

- **One price per size**: every MIOSA plan pays the same hourly price for a size, plus the same rates for disk and egress; plans only change caps and concurrency. Developer hard-stops at a $0 balance.
- **Sandboxes, computers, and deployments** on one API, with [white-label branding](/docs/platform/white-label) for your own customers.
- **Bring your own hardware or cloud**: [OpenComputers](/docs/opencomputers) and [Bring your own cloud](/docs/infrastructure/byoc/overview).
- **Capabilities and measured performance**: see [MIOSA vs other platforms](/docs/compare) and the [Benchmarks](/docs/benchmarks).

## Sources

- MIOSA: live pricing API, `GET https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/compute/pricing` (checked 2026-10-20); [Pricing and limits](/docs/pricing).
- Freestyle: https://www.freestyle.sh/pricing (checked 2026-10-20).

- Vercel Sandbox: https://vercel.com/docs/vercel-sandbox/pricing (checked 2026-10-20).
- Capabilities and measured performance: [MIOSA vs other platforms](/docs/compare).

> **Caution**
>
> Pricing and capabilities change.

integrations/examples:
Four complete, runnable examples. Each demonstrates a different frontend stack and a different set of white-label capabilities. Clone the repo and follow the "Run locally" steps below each entry.

Every example should pass three proofs before you adapt it: the application starts locally, its MIOSA resource resolves to the intended Workspace and Project, and the browser never receives a server API key.

## Pick an example

| Goal | Start with | Completion proof |
|---|---|---|
| Server-rendered integration | `whitelabel-saas` | A customer Sandbox opens through a scoped Preview token |
| React product with embedded terminal | `whitelabel-react-saas` | Refresh resumes the same attributed Sandbox |
| Next.js marketplace or builder | `whitelabel-nextjs-marketplace` | Multiple Projects remain separated by canonical IDs |
| Vue learning environment | `whitelabel-vue-tutor` | Quotas and teardown apply to the correct end user |

> **Caution: Use examples as executable starting points**
>
> Run the example unchanged first.
> Record the successful local URL and MIOSA resource IDs, then adapt one concern at a time.

All examples live in `examples/` at the root of the [MIOSA GitHub repository](https://github.com/Miosa-osa/miosa).

---

## whitelabel-saas

**Stack:** Python (Flask) backend + plain HTML/JS frontend

**What it demonstrates:**

- One-time tenant setup: custom preview domain, branding, webhook registration
- Per-customer sandbox provisioning with `external_user_id`, `external_project_id`, and `metadata`
- Server-side preview token minting and iframe embed
- HMAC-SHA256 webhook signature verification
- Teardown by `external_user_id` (cancellation flow)

This is the canonical reference example. Every concept in the [white-label walkthrough](/docs/platform/white-label) maps directly to code in this example.

**Run locally:**

```bash
cd examples/whitelabel-saas
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

cp .env.example .env
# Edit .env  -  fill in MIOSA_API_KEY

python setup.py      # one-time tenant setup
python app.py        # server on http://localhost:8000
# Open index.html in a browser for the embed demo
```

**GitHub:** [`examples/whitelabel-saas`](https://github.com/Miosa-osa/miosa/tree/main/examples/whitelabel-saas)

---

## whitelabel-react-saas

**Stack:** React 18 (Vite) frontend + Express.js BFF

**What it demonstrates:**

- BFF pattern: Express mints browser tokens; React uses `@miosa/sdk` directly in the browser
- Live terminal inside an iframe powered by the TypeScript SDK
- Per-user sandbox state stored in the BFF session
- Sandbox resume on page refresh (poll for `state === "running"` before showing the embed)
- Token refresh on `miosa:preview:expired` message event

**Run locally:**

```bash
cd examples/whitelabel-react-saas
pnpm install

cp .env.example .env
# Edit .env  -  fill in MIOSA_API_KEY

pnpm dev   # starts both Express (port 3001) and Vite (port 5173)
# Open http://localhost:5173
```

**GitHub:** [`examples/whitelabel-react-saas`](https://github.com/Miosa-osa/miosa/tree/main/examples/whitelabel-react-saas)

---

## whitelabel-nextjs-marketplace

**Stack:** Next.js 15 (App Router) full-stack

**What it demonstrates:**

- Next.js Route Handlers as the BFF: token minting without a separate Express server
- Seller onboarding: sandbox provisioned on first login, re-used on return
- Multi-project listing: sandboxes filtered by `external_user_id` and rendered as cards
- Usage display: per-seller compute hours fetched with `client.usage.get(external_user_id)`
- Custom `next.config.js` to proxy sandbox previews through the Next.js server (avoid CORS for embedded iframes)

**Run locally:**

```bash
cd examples/whitelabel-nextjs-marketplace
pnpm install

cp .env.local.example .env.local
# Edit .env.local  -  fill in MIOSA_API_KEY

pnpm dev   # starts on http://localhost:3000
```

**GitHub:** [`examples/whitelabel-nextjs-marketplace`](https://github.com/Miosa-osa/miosa/tree/main/examples/whitelabel-nextjs-marketplace)

---

## whitelabel-vue-tutor

**Stack:** Vue 3 (Vite) frontend + Express.js backend

**What it demonstrates:**

- Per-lesson sandbox lifecycle: fresh sandbox per lesson, destroyed on completion
- Quota enforcement: custom middleware rejects `sandbox.create` if the user has reached their limit
- Public share links with a 15-minute TTL for peer review
- File-tree component: reads the sandbox filesystem via `client.files.list(sandboxId, "/")`
- Run-button component: streams exec output via `client.exec.stream(sandboxId, "npm test")`

**Run locally:**

```bash
cd examples/whitelabel-vue-tutor
pnpm install

cp .env.example .env
# Edit .env  -  fill in MIOSA_API_KEY

pnpm dev   # starts both Express (port 3001) and Vite (port 5174)
# Open http://localhost:5174
```

**GitHub:** [`examples/whitelabel-vue-tutor`](https://github.com/Miosa-osa/miosa/tree/main/examples/whitelabel-vue-tutor)

---

| Live terminal |  -  | Yes |  -  | Yes |
| File tree |  -  |  -  |  -  | Yes |
| Exec streaming |  -  |  -  |  -  | Yes |
| Usage display |  -  |  -  | Yes |  -  |
| Quota enforcement |  -  |  -  |  -  | Yes |
| Public share links |  -  |  -  |  -  | Yes |
| Teardown by user | Yes |  -  |  -  |  -  |

## Contributing an example

If you build something on MIOSA and want to share it, open a pull request in the [MIOSA GitHub repository](https://github.com/Miosa-osa/miosa). Examples must:

- Include a working `README.md` with local setup instructions
- Not commit `MIOSA_API_KEY` or any secrets
- Use `external_user_id` for all resource attribution
- Verify webhook signatures if a webhook endpoint is included
- Include a smoke command that exits nonzero when the primary user journey fails
- Pin supported runtime and package-manager versions
- Explain expected output and cleanup steps

---

integrations/external-computers:
MIOSA runs your workloads on its own cloud by default, and it can also run them on hardware you own or operate yourself.
Two bring-your-own paths are supported today.
Connecting a third-party sandbox or desktop provider such as Orgo, E2B, or Daytona is **not** supported today: those adapters are not part of the product.

## Where compute can run

| Source | Status | Where it runs |
|---|---|---|
| MIOSA cloud | Available | MIOSA-managed sandboxes and computers |
| OpenComputers | Available | Hardware you own or rent, connected over an outbound WebSocket |
| Bring your own cloud | Available, by onboarding | Worker capacity inside your own AWS or Google Cloud account |
| Third-party provider adapter | Not offered | - |

Sandboxes run on Firecracker by default.
SOMA is available to every customer, and `auto` lets the platform choose.
See [Choosing a runtime](/docs/soma/choosing-a-runtime).

## Run on hardware you own

[OpenComputers](/docs/opencomputers) is MIOSA's bring-your-own-hardware path.
You run a small host agent on a machine you control, and it enrolls with MIOSA over an outbound WebSocket.
The machine then appears to your application with the same interface as a MIOSA computer, so your product drives both without branching on the host.
Start with [Connect a host](/docs/opencomputers/connect).

## Run in your own cloud account

For worker capacity inside your own AWS or Google Cloud account, MIOSA has a separate onboarding path.
See [Bring your own cloud](/docs/infrastructure/byoc/overview).

## What is not offered

MIOSA does not currently provide adapters that connect a third-party compute provider.
There is no supported way to drive an Orgo, E2B, Daytona, or similar machine through the MIOSA API today, and you cannot connect a third-party API key to run machines inside MIOSA.

> **Note: Use a supported path instead**
>
> If you need capacity outside the MIOSA cloud, use [OpenComputers](/docs/opencomputers) on hardware you control, or [Bring your own cloud](/docs/infrastructure/byoc/overview) in your own cloud account.

## See also

- [Computers overview](/docs/computers/overview)  -  the unified computer surface
- [Sandboxes](/docs/develop/sandboxes)  -  isolated, disposable code execution
- [OpenComputers](/docs/opencomputers)  -  bring your own hardware
- [Bring your own cloud](/docs/infrastructure/byoc/overview)  -  worker capacity in your own cloud account
- [Compute provider comparison](/docs/integrations/comparison)  -  how MIOSA's rates compare
integrations/webhooks:
MIOSA sends HTTP `POST` requests to your endpoint whenever a sandbox or deployment changes state. Use webhooks to update your database, notify users, trigger downstream actions, or bill for compute.

---

## Event taxonomy

### Sandbox events

| Event | Fires when |
|---|---|
| `sandbox.created` | The sandbox row is inserted. The VM may still be booting. |
| `sandbox.running` | The sandbox is fully booted and ready. `external_user_id` is available. |
| `sandbox.paused` | The sandbox was paused due to an idle timeout or an explicit API call. |
| `sandbox.resumed` | A paused sandbox was resumed. |
| `sandbox.destroyed` | The sandbox was permanently deleted. |
| `sandbox.error` | The sandbox failed to boot or encountered a runtime error. |

### Deployment events

| Event | Fires when |
|---|---|
| `deployment.created` | A new deployment was created. |
| `deployment.build_started` | A build started for a new version. |
| `deployment.build_succeeded` | A build finished successfully. |
| `deployment.build_failed` | A build failed. The `error` field contains the failure reason. |
| `deployment.published` | A version was promoted to the active release. |
| `deployment.domain_attached` | A custom domain was verified and attached. |

### Forge events

Every Forge event names its repository in the payload (`repository.id`, `repository.full_name`, `repository.owner`, `repository.slug`), so one organization subscription can route events from every repository. Subscriptions cannot be limited to a single repository.

| Event | Fires when |
|---|---|
| `forge.push` | A push to a repository was accepted. |
| `forge.pull_request` | A pull request was opened, closed, reopened, merged or reviewed. |
| `forge.check` | A check reported on a pull request or a commit. The payload includes `commit_sha`. |

---

## Payload structure

Every webhook delivery has the same envelope:

```json
{
  "id": "evt_01hzqmrkntq6g9gxnqhvpa8c7t",
  "type": "sandbox.running",
  "created_at": "2026-05-25T14:32:10Z",
  "data": {
    "id": "sbx_01hzq5pnmpgt6vdwp0r8d23c5n",
    "state": "running",
    "external_user_id": "user_42",
    "external_project_id": "proj_lumen_1",
    "metadata": {
      "customer_id": "user_42",
      "project_name": "brand-refresh",
      "source": "lumen-whitelabel"
    },
    "preview_url": "https://3000-sbx01hzq.sandbox.example.com"
  }
}
```

The `id` field is a unique event ID. Use it to deduplicate deliveries.

---

## HMAC-SHA256 signature verification

Every delivery includes a `Miosa-Signature` header:

```yaml
Miosa-Signature: t=1716645130,v1=a3f2c8...
```

- `t`  -  Unix timestamp (seconds) when MIOSA signed the request
- `v1`  -  HMAC-SHA256 hex digest of `"<t>.<raw_body>"`

The signed payload is `timestamp + "." + raw request body bytes`. Verify before parsing the JSON.

> **Caution: Replay protection**
>
> Reject events where the timestamp `t` is more than 300 seconds (5 minutes) in the past or future. This prevents replay attacks using captured valid signatures.

**Python**

```python
import hashlib
import hmac
import time

def verify_miosa_signature(body: bytes, header: str, secret: str) -> bool:
    """Return True if the signature is valid."""
    try:
        parts = dict(item.split("=", 1) for item in header.split(","))
        timestamp = parts["t"]
        received = parts["v1"]
    except (KeyError, ValueError):
        return False

    # Reject stale events.
    if abs(time.time() - int(timestamp)) > 300:
        return False

    signed = f"{timestamp}.{body.decode('utf-8')}"
    expected = hmac.new(
        secret.encode("utf-8"),
        signed.encode("utf-8"),
        hashlib.sha256,
    ).hexdigest()

    return hmac.compare_digest(expected, received)

# Flask example
from flask import request, jsonify

@app.post("/webhooks/miosa")
def miosa_webhook():
    raw = request.get_data()
    sig = request.headers.get("Miosa-Signature", "")

    if not verify_miosa_signature(raw, sig, WEBHOOK_SECRET):
        return jsonify({"error": "invalid signature"}), 401

    event = request.get_json()
    handle_event(event)
    return jsonify({"ok": True}), 200
```

**TypeScript**

```typescript
import crypto from "node:crypto";
import type { Request, Response } from "express";

function verifyMiosaSignature(
  rawBody: Buffer,
  header: string,
  secret: string,
): boolean {
  const parts = Object.fromEntries(
    header.split(",").map((p) => p.split("=") as [string, string]),
  );
  const { t: timestamp, v1: received } = parts;
  if (!timestamp || !received) return false;

  // Reject stale events.
  if (Math.abs(Date.now() / 1000 - Number(timestamp)) > 300) return false;

  const signed = `${timestamp}.${rawBody.toString("utf8")}`;
  const expected = crypto
    .createHmac("sha256", secret)
    .update(signed)
    .digest("hex");

  return crypto.timingSafeEqual(
    Buffer.from(expected, "hex"),
    Buffer.from(received, "hex"),
  );
}

// Express example
app.post("/webhooks/miosa", express.raw({ type: "*/*" }), (req: Request, res: Response) => {
  const sig = req.headers["miosa-signature"] as string ?? "";
  if (!verifyMiosaSignature(req.body, sig, process.env.MIOSA_WEBHOOK_SECRET!)) {
    return res.status(401).json({ error: "invalid signature" });
  }
  const event = JSON.parse(req.body.toString());
  handleEvent(event);
  res.json({ ok: true });
});
```

**Go**

```go
package main

import (
    "crypto/hmac"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "math"
    "net/http"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func verifyMiosaSignature(body []byte, header, secret string) bool {
    parts := map[string]string{}
    for _, part := range strings.Split(header, ",") {
        kv := strings.SplitN(part, "=", 2)
        if len(kv) == 2 {
            parts[kv[0]] = kv[1]
        }
    }
    ts, ok1 := parts["t"]
    received, ok2 := parts["v1"]
    if !ok1 || !ok2 {
        return false
    }

    tsInt, err := strconv.ParseInt(ts, 10, 64)
    if err != nil || math.Abs(float64(time.Now().Unix()-tsInt)) > 300 {
        return false
    }

    signed := fmt.Sprintf("%s.%s", ts, string(body))
    mac := hmac.New(sha256.New, []byte(secret))
    mac.Write([]byte(signed))
    expected := hex.EncodeToString(mac.Sum(nil))

    return hmac.Equal([]byte(expected), []byte(received))
}

func webhookHandler(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    body, _ := io.ReadAll(r.Body)
    sig := r.Header.Get("Miosa-Signature")

    if !verifyMiosaSignature(body, sig, webhookSecret) {
        http.Error(w, "invalid signature", http.StatusUnauthorized)
        return
    }

    // parse and handle body ...
    w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)
}
```

## Idempotency

MIOSA may deliver the same event more than once (network retries, at-least-once semantics). Make your handler idempotent by storing the event `id` and discarding duplicates:

```python
processed_events = set()  # use a database or cache in production

def handle_event(event: dict) -> None:
    event_id = event["id"]
    if event_id in processed_events:
        return  # duplicate  -  skip
    processed_events.add(event_id)

    match event["type"]:
        case "sandbox.running":
            notify_user(event["data"]["external_user_id"])
        case "sandbox.destroyed":
            release_resources(event["data"]["id"])
        case "sandbox.error":
            alert_oncall(event["data"])
```

## Retry policy

| Attempt | Delay |
|---|---|
| 1 (initial) | Immediate |
| 2 | 1 minute |
| 3 | 5 minutes |
| 4 | 30 minutes |
| 5 | 1 hour |
| 6 | 2 hours |
| 7 | 4 hours |
| 8 | 8 hours |

MIOSA makes up to eight delivery attempts over roughly 15.5 hours (within a 24-hour window), then drops the event. If your endpoint is unreachable, check the webhook delivery log in the MIOSA dashboard.

Return a `2xx` status code within **10 seconds** to acknowledge receipt. If your processing takes longer, acknowledge immediately and handle the event asynchronously.

```python
hook = client.webhooks.create(
```

## Local testing

Use a tunnel to expose your local server during development:

```bash
# Option 1  -  ngrok
ngrok http 8000
# Copy the https URL, set MIOSA_WEBHOOK_URL in .env

# Option 2  -  cloudflared
cloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:8000
```

Then run the one-time setup script to register the tunnel URL as your webhook endpoint. When you restart the tunnel and get a new URL, update the webhook:

```python
# Update an existing webhook's URL
client.webhooks.update("whk_abc123", url="https://new-tunnel.ngrok.io/webhooks/miosa")
```
